pharm: Concentration-dependent bactericidal aminoglycoside that binds irreversibly to the 30S bacterial ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and inhibition of protein synthesis, with broad activity against aerobic gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
quick: 3 mg/kg/day IM/IV in 2-3 divided doses (up to 4-5 mg/kg/day in severe infection)
Avoid - aminoglycosides risk fetal ototoxicity; use only if essential
Minimal oral absorption by infant; use with caution
Reduce dose / extend interval; guided by levels and CrCl
No direct interaction; avoid in acute illness
summary: Sisomicin is a parenteral aminoglycoside antibiotic, closely related to gentamicin, with potent concentration-dependent bactericidal activity against aerobic gram-negative bacilli, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacteriaceae, and (in synergy with a beta-lactam) some gram-positive organisms. It is used for serious systemic gram-negative infections. Like all aminoglycosides, it carries significant risks of dose- and duration-related nephrotoxicity and irreversible ototoxicity (cochlear and vestibular), and it can cause neuromuscular blockade. Dosing requires weight-based calculation, renal-function adjustment, and therapeutic drug monitoring. It is used in some countries (notably parts of Europe and Asia) and is not currently FDA-approved in the United States.
indications: Serious gram-negative bacterial infections, including septicemia, complicated urinary tract infections, lower respiratory tract infections, intra-abdominal infections, and skin/soft-tissue and bone infections caused by susceptible organisms (often in combination with a beta-lactam)

dosage.n: Base on ideal/adjusted body weight; verify with drug levels

dosage.d: Up to 4-5 mg/kg/day in divided doses, reduced once clinically improved
dosage.n: Higher dose only short-term with close monitoring
Dose by weight and adjust to levels

dosage.d: Reduce dose and/or extend dosing interval according to creatinine clearance
dosage.n: Adjust using measured peak and trough concentrations

admin: Give by deep intramuscular injection or by slow intravenous infusion (over 30-60 minutes)
Calculate dose on ideal or adjusted body weight and patient renal function
Ensure adequate hydration before and during therapy to reduce nephrotoxicity
Do not physically mix in the same syringe/infusion with beta-lactam antibiotics (inactivation)
Monitor serum peak and trough concentrations, renal function, and hearing/balance during treatment
moa: Sisomicin is an aminoglycoside that exerts concentration-dependent bactericidal activity. It is actively transported across the bacterial cell envelope (an oxygen-dependent process, hence limited activity against anaerobes) and binds irreversibly to the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome. This binding causes misreading of the genetic code, premature termination, and incorporation of incorrect amino acids into proteins, producing nonfunctional or aberrant proteins and disrupting the cytoplasmic membrane. The resulting membrane damage allows further drug uptake and leads to rapid bacterial death. Its activity is enhanced when combined with cell-wall-active agents such as beta-lactams (synergy).

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to sisomicin or other aminoglycosides
relative: Concurrent other nephrotoxic, ototoxic, or neuromuscular-blocking agents
monitor: Serum peak and trough drug concentrations
Signs of neuromuscular weakness, especially with anesthetics/muscle relaxants

preg: Aminoglycosides cross the placenta and can cause irreversible bilateral congenital deafness in the fetus. Sisomicin should be avoided in pregnancy and used only when there is no safer alternative and the benefit clearly outweighs the fetal risk.
lact: Aminoglycosides are excreted in breast milk in small amounts and are poorly absorbed orally by the infant; however, use with caution and monitor the infant for possible effects on gut flora (diarrhea, thrush).
renal: Sisomicin is eliminated almost entirely by the kidneys and accumulates in renal impairment, increasing nephro- and ototoxicity. Reduce the dose and/or lengthen the dosing interval according to creatinine clearance and adjust using measured serum peak and trough levels. Maintain adequate hydration and monitor renal function throughout therapy.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment, as the drug is cleared renally rather than hepatically.

major: Other nephrotoxic agents (amphotericin B, vancomycin, cisplatin, ciclosporin, foscarnet) - additive nephrotoxicity
Other ototoxic agents and potent loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid) - additive ototoxicity
Neuromuscular blocking agents and anesthetics - potentiated neuromuscular blockade / respiratory paralysis
moderate: Beta-lactam antibiotics - synergistic antibacterial effect, but mutual inactivation if mixed in the same solution; administer separately
NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin in neonates) - may increase aminoglycoside levels
minor: Bisphosphonates - additive hypocalcemia/hypomagnesemia reported with aminoglycosides
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; avoid alcohol during acute serious infection.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia) and elevations in serum creatinine and urea.

serious: Nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis, acute kidney injury)
Ototoxicity - irreversible cochlear (hearing loss) and vestibular (vertigo, ataxia) damage
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions including rash and fever

monitoring: Serum peak and trough concentrations (efficacy and toxicity)
Renal function (creatinine, urea, urine output) at baseline and during therapy
Audiometry and vestibular assessment, especially with prolonged therapy
Signs of neuromuscular weakness, particularly perioperatively
counsel: This antibiotic is given by injection or drip in a healthcare setting
Report any ringing in the ears, hearing loss, dizziness, or unsteadiness immediately
Tell staff about reduced urine output or swelling - your kidneys will be checked
Inform your doctor of all other medicines, especially diuretics or other antibiotics
Hearing and kidney tests may be done during a longer course of treatment
Let staff know if you have muscle weakness or have had myasthenia gravis
pk: Rapid bactericidal effect; peak serum levels ~30-60 min after IM dose
Therapeutic peak typically ~4-10 mcg/mL (target per regimen)
Concentration-dependent killing with post-antibiotic effect; dosed every 8-12 h
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light per product
pearls: Closely related to gentamicin; concentration-dependent bactericidal aminoglycoside with anti-Pseudomonas activity
Nephrotoxicity and irreversible ototoxicity are the key dose/duration-related risks - monitor levels, renal and auditory function
Poor activity against anaerobes (uptake is oxygen-dependent) and limited activity at acidic/abscess sites
Synergistic with beta-lactams but must NOT be mixed in the same infusion (mutual inactivation)
Avoid in myasthenia gravis and with neuromuscular blockers - risk of paralysis
Regulatory status: used in some European/Asian countries; not FDA-approved in the US - guidance from SmPC/BNF and aminoglycoside class data
missed: As this is a clinician-administered parenteral antibiotic, a missed dose should be given as soon as recognized and the dosing schedule adjusted by the prescriber; do not double up. Trough timing relative to the next dose should be reconsidered if the schedule is altered.
overdose: Overdose or accumulation causes nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade. Management is supportive: discontinue the drug, ensure hydration, and treat neuromuscular blockade with calcium salts and ventilatory support as needed. Hemodialysis (or hemofiltration) effectively removes sisomicin and can be used in serious overdose or renal failure.
